11502-an-englishman-looks-at-the-world-b:
H. G. Wells's 1914 Englishman Looks at the World gathers unrestrained remarks on contemporary matters in twenty-six essays. Starting with Blériot's flight and its consequences for cheap travel, Wells considers the king and a new epoch, empire, labour unrest, socialism, modern warfare, the novel. the public library, Chesterton and Belloc, Sir Thomas More, London traffic, sociology, divorce, schoolmasters, motherhood, doctors, specialization, parliaments, American population, civilizational collapse, and the ideal citizen.

Wells writes as a prophet of the new age, confident and combative. The collection shows Edwardian progressive thought just before the war tested it. Readers of Wells's nonfiction will find here his breadth: aviation, politics, literature, and social reform in one restless volume.
11890-comrades-of-the-saddle-or-the-youn:
Frank V. Webster's 1910 boys' book, subtitled The Young Rough Riders of the Plains, follows a group of young riders on the western plains. Webster, already known for school and farm stories such as Only a Farm Boy and Tom the Telephone Boy, writes for readers who liked horses, camps, and quick action.

Chapters show the boys packing saddle bags with food, plates, coffee, and blankets, buckling on cartridge belts, and riding out with rifles across their shoulders. Talk of ranch deals and bragging heard in El Paso gives the adventure a plot beyond the trail, as the riders test themselves against older men who doubt them.
13603-the-hawaiian-romance-of-laieikawai:
Martha Warren Beckwith gives the Hawaiian romance of Laieikawai with introduction and translation, illustrated by a kahuna or native sorcerer. Conclusions, persons, action, and background precede text and translation, from the princess's birth and flight to Paliuli through wooing, boxing, and the house thatched with bird feathers.

Aiwohikupua goes to woo the princess, deserts his sisters, and meets the guardians of Paliuli, while Kahalaomapuana. The princess's war chief, warns Hauailiki to go back or birds of Paliuli will eat his flesh. Hauailiki flees to Keaau by early morning. Beckwith preserves a Hawaiian chiefly romance in both languages, with scholarship that lets English readers follow its gods, chiefs, and customs.
16233-an-essay-towards-fixing-the-true-s:
First printed in 1744 and reprinted in 1947 by the Augustan Reprint Society, this essay tries to fix true standards for wit, humor, raillery, satire, and ridicule. James L. Clifford supplies an introduction and a bibliographical note, placing the short work among eighteenth-century debates about taste. The Augustan editors present it as a text worth study, priced at one dollar.

Its opening pages tease the flattery of dedications, noting that writers in dedications, like carvers of tomb inscriptions, seldom tell hard truths. The essay then sorts kinds of comic writing with Augustan care for definition. Students of satire, rhetoric, and eighteenth-century letters will find a compact, witty specimen.
20184-the-adventures-of-uncle-jeremiah-a:
Uncle Jeremiah and his family visit the great fair in this comic tale. He rides in comfort and marvels at the age of travel. All nations feed our appetites, he says in wonder and pride. Millions are spent to carry us in ease, he tells a stranger.

He travels with Sarah and Mary's two children toward the fair. Great fairs drew farm families to gape at machines, foods, and nations. The tale turns their wonder into gentle, folksy comedy throughout. Readers get a period snapshot of rural folk meeting the modern world.
21319-three-boys-or-the-chiefs-of-the-cl:
A nearly ruined castle on Scotland's northwest coast houses the chiefs of the Clan Mackhai in George Manville Fenn's tale. Max, a London lawyer's son, is sent to stay there because the chief has borrowed heavily from Max's father and not repaid. The chief's son Kenneth and his gillie put Max through test after test of bravery.

Slaps, kicks, and Highland tempers fly from the first chapter, with young Scoodrach caught between the boys. Behind the sport sits real money trouble: the castle itself is under threat of seizure for debt. Fenn mixes peril after peril with clan pride, and the end follows plainly once Max learns what his visit means.
25708-the-hero-of-ticonderoga-or-ethan-a:
John De Morgan writes this boys' history tale, The Hero of Ticonderoga, or Ethan Allen and his Green Mountain Boys, published in Philadelphia by David McKay in 1896. De Morgan, author of Paul Revere and The First Shot for Liberty, fronts the book with a wallet drawn silently by a stick.

Chapters open at the courthouse, with the Green Mountain Boys, a child of nature, and the rising of the moon. Defiance, an ambuscade, a convention, and treachery follow. Zeb's double dealing and the tables turned lead to war, Benedict Arnold, and the hero of Ticonderoga itself, with Crown Point and news from Boston.
29349-creatures-of-the-night-a-book-of-w:
Alfred W. Rees, author of Ianto the Fisherman and Other Sketches of Country Life, published this book of wild life in western Britain with John Murray in London. Rees writes natural history biography, following animals through their nights and seasons rather than listing species. Press notices quoted in the volume praise the book highly, with the Guardian finding nothing recent to compare with its first part.

Contents follow the otter to its holt among the alders, the pool beneath the farmstead, and the gorge of Alltycafn. The water-vole, village hounds, and a burrow in the river bank also appear. Readers get a lyrical nature book of western Britain, attentive to field, moor, and river, and to the night creatures that own them after dark.
34269-rookie-rhymes-by-the-men-of-the-1s:
Men of the first and second provisional training regiments at Plattsburg, New York, wrote verses between May and August 1917. Harper and Brothers published the book that September. A foreword by Robert Tapley opens the poems. Morris Bishop contributes Standing in Line and Inoculation Day, among other pieces.

Poems cover the first time in uniform, Sunday in barracks, and the manual of arms. Others treat patriotic songs, a troopship chanty, and the horrors of war. Named writers give their company and regiment with each piece. The rhymes are comic, homesick, and proud by turns. They record how new officers in training saw camp life.
34787-fish-populations-following-a-droug:
James Deacon wrote on fish populations following a drought, in 1961. The University of Kansas printed the study at Lawrence that year. It stands in the museum of natural history publications, volume thirteen. Two Kansas rivers are its ground, the Neosho and the Marais des Cygnes. A state biological survey shared the work with a game commission.

Methods open the contents of the long paper. Electrical fishing gear, seines, and gill nets are described there. Sodium cyanide, rotenone, and dyes stand among its tools also. Determination of abundance and the names of fishes follow in order. An annotated list of species fills the great body of the work. The fish-fauna of the upper Neosho is treated after the list. Descriptions of the two rivers and their study areas stand early. Deacon gives drought's ledger on two prairie rivers.
37111-the-zankiwank-and-the-bletherwitch:
The Zankiwank and the Bletherwitch, an original fantastic fairy extravaganza by Fitzgerald with pictures by Arthur Rackham, was published by Dent at London in 1896. A Ruskin motto heads the title page, declaring imagination the ruling and divine power in man.

The book falls into four parts: a trip to Fable Land, the fairies' feather and flower land, a visit to Shadow Land, and the land of Topsy Turvey. Its illustration list promises the Jackarandajam, a demon on a bicycle, frogs playing kiss in the ring, an elfin orchestra, and fairies leaping from flower petals. Rackham's pictures, including a frontispiece of everybody rushing for the train, carry the nonsense as much as the text.
37286-tales-from-jo-kai:
Tales from Jokai gathers stories by Maurus Jokai, translated from the Hungarian by Nisbet Bain. Jarrold and Sons of London published the volume, here in its third edition. A complete biography and a photogravure portrait of the author accompany the tales.

The publisher's list names Jokai's other novels in English. They include A Hungarian Nabob, Black Diamonds, The Nameless Castle, and The Lion of Janina. Front matter traces the author's career from a Hungarian Academy meeting in 1843. Bain, the translator, was the chief English champion of Hungarian letters. The collection gave English readers a path into the work of Hungary's most popular novelist. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
37589-through-magic-glasses-and-other-le:
Through Magic Glasses, by Arabella Buckley, was published in 1890. Appleton issued the authorized edition at New York. The lectures form a sequel to The Fairyland of Science. A photograph of the great nebula in Orion fronts the book. Isaac Roberts took it in February 1889. Buckley's preface addresses her young friends directly. The volume shows marvels that optical instruments open to study. Each subject, she warns, could fill a lifetime of work. Her little account is meant to make readers long for more. Cheap instruments and good lectures are now in reach, she notes.

Some eager minds may take up a branch of this unseen world. The last two lectures stray from the glasses, to close a Devonshire course. One treats fungi, first printed in a shorter form. Buckley writes science as story for the young.
4068-froudacity-west-indian-fables-by-ja:
A reply to James Anthony Froude's West Indian fables, prefaced by J. J. Thomas, answers the historian's account of the islands. The book follows Froude's voyage out through Barbados, St. Vincent, and Grenada, then turns to Trinidad and its struggle for political enfranchisement.

Thomas argues that Froude's scheme for future rule arrived out of season, and that the gentlemen of Trinidad would meet his historical self-praise with indignant contempt. The work is a sharp colonial rebuttal, written in 1888's heat. Readers interested in Caribbean history will find a direct, angry answer to an imperial traveler.
44053-sermons-selected-from-the-papers-o:
Sermons Selected from the Papers of the Late Reverend Clement Bailhache gathers the preaching of a minister whose notes his editor found nearly ready for the press. The Reverend J P Barnett edited the volume, and Elliot Stock of Paternoster Row, London, published it in 1880. A portrait of Bailhache, photographed at Huddersfield, forms the frontispiece, under the motto of work too fair to die.

The sixteen sermons follow their texts. Salvation, Propitiation, and Faith in the Saviour open the course, from Titus, John, and Acts. Consecration, Christianity in Our Daily Life, Unconscious Influence, and Secular Anxiety press the faith into weekday practice. Contentment, Joy, Sickness, Prayer, and Assurance close the list. The editor's note praises a preacher who never allowed himself to think superficially or write carelessly, and whose papers needed almost nothing done to them.
44815-writing-and-drawing-made-easy-amus:
An engraved school book teaches writing and drawing through emblems and moral copies, sold at Kingston upon Thames. The whole alphabet appears in all the letter forms then used, in print and in penmanship. Each letter is matched with an emblem picture and a moral copy line for pupils to trace.

The preface offers the book as a help to schoolmasters, saving them time in setting copies. Most copies were first written by William Chinnery Senior, an able penman, then engraved by a noted artist. A long list of subscribers, from tradesmen to ladies of rank, heads the volume. Readers get a window on Georgian schooling, where a fair hand, a drawn line, and a moral lesson were taught as one art.
46205-jack-among-the-indians-or-a-boy-s-:
Jack Among the Indians, or A Boy's Summer on the Buffalo Plains, is George Bird Grinnell's sequel for boys. Stokes printed it in New York in 1900, with pictures by Edwin Willard Deming. A frontispiece shows Jack firing.

A letter to his nephews and nieces, dated September 1900, opens the book. Long ago, Grinnell writes, buffalo herds fed on the plains. The Indians lived by hunting them: flesh for food, skins for clothes and lodges, tools from the body. Few settlements stood, and tribes followed the herds over the land. War journeys and hunting adventures broke the quiet of village life. Jack, of the Young Ranchman book, spends this summer with the buffalo eaters. He hunts their game, fights their enemies, and lives their life. The chapters run from the ranch to the first fresh meat.
47129-flying-the-atlantic-in-sixteen-hou:
Flying the Atlantic in Sixteen Hours is an account by Sir Arthur Whitten Brown, aided by Captain Alan Bott. Brown was navigator of the first nonstop Atlantic flight. Twenty one photos picture the book. The New York edition was copyrighted in nineteen twenty. A portrait of Brown serves as frontispiece. Contents split the flight into stages: preliminary events, the start, evening, night, morning, and the arrival.

Later chapters treat the navigation of aircraft and the future of transatlantic flight. The air age closes the book. It is an awful thing to be told one has made history, Brown begins. Such a charge implies a duty to live up to other people's expectations, he writes. An ordinary person who has been lucky cannot fulfil it, he owns. Photos show the machine being set up at the Newfoundland start.
50390-a-history-of-sinai:
Lina Eckenstein, who wrote Woman Under Monasticism, traced the long past of Sinai in this book. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge printed it in London in 1921, with maps and plates. Eckenstein dated her preface at Easter 1920.

Her chart of Egyptian reigns starts deep in time, with the first line of kings set near 5500 BC. Stones of Semerkhet and Khufu in Sinai mark the early age. The Hyksos conquest, the time of Abraham and Joseph, and the age of Moses all find their place. Lists of the bishops of Pharan and of Sinai, from the year 869 on, show the church age of the holy mountain.
54977-the-sovereignty-of-the-sea-an-hist:
The Sovereignty of the Sea is a history of England's claims to rule the British seas, by Thomas Wemyss Fulton. Fulton lectured on fishery problems at the University of Aberdeen. Blackwood published the book at Edinburgh and London in 1911, with pictures. A map shows the British seas as the lawyer Selden once drew them.

In his preface Fulton says he first meant to treat the subject through fisheries alone. He widened the plan, since fishing was never the only matter at stake. Trade, sea law, and the naval salute to the flag were bound up with the claim. The book falls into two parts. The first traces the old pretensions to dominion of the sea. The second treats what survives of them, the territorial waters, under the law of nations and the rights of fishing.
57269-terra-australis-incognita-or-a-new:
Terra Australis Incognita tells of a fifth part of the world found south. Ferdinand de Quir, a Spanish captain, brought the strange news home. The tale was first printed in sixteen hundred seventeen and reprinted here. William Bray sold the London form from Exeter Court in the Strand.

Peter Ferdinand de Quir begs the King of Spain in this plea. It is his eighth such plea, he tells the crown with plain grief. Fourteen months he has waited at court for one firm word back. Fourteen years he has spent on the search, through a thousand perils. His purse is sunk, his frame worn, his crosses past belief, he says. Send colonies to the rich, fruitful south land, he begs the king. God’s glory and Spain’s gain both hang on the bold design. No answer had yet crowned his pains when this plea was penned.
6094-the-scouts-of-stonewall-the-story-o:
Joseph A. Altsheler continues his Civil War series with The Scouts of Stonewall, the story of the Great Valley campaign. Though an independent story, it follows The Guns of Bull Run and The Guns of Shiloh, reverting to the Southern side and the fortunes of Harry Kenton and his friends.

Harry fights for the South while his cousin Dick Mason fights for the North, with Colonel Kenton, Mrs. Mason, Juliana, and officers of both armies around them. Later volumes carry the series to Antietam, Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and Appomattox. Altsheler writes boy-centered war romance with maps of loyalty and kin.
61599-the-gardens-of-the-sun-a-naturalis:
Burbidge roams the east in The Gardens of the Sun, a naturalist's journal on the mountains and in the forests and swamps of Borneo and the Sulu Archipelago. Murray of London prints the book in 1880, with plates. Burbidge served the botanical gardens of Trinity College, Dublin, and had served the Royal Gardens at Kew.

He gives the work to his wife, since while he worked abroad she waited at home, the dedication says. His first word frames the Malay islands as the Gardens of the Sun. Nature is ever beautiful there, and man, though often primitive, is kind to the stranger, he writes. A few weeks of sea brings the traveller to an always afternoon climate, he says, where winter is unknown.
61930-observations-on-the-state-of-relig:
Observations on the State of Religion and Literature in Spain is a travel report of 1819. Smallfield printed it in London that year. It records a trip through the peninsula. The author counts two hundred thousand clergy in Spain. Their revenues are immense, he says. Their hold on the people, though, is waning. The government still props their authority up.

He is careful to split the clergy into kinds. Parish priests are mostly humane and learned, he finds. Many of them favour liberty and letters. The monks and friars draw his scorn instead. Rich convents hoard wealth while mendicants beg. Ignorance and idleness rule those orders, he charges. Their power rests on the people's degradation. The book is a liberal Protestant's view of Spain. It belongs to the years after the Peninsular War.
62128-a-grammar-of-colloquial-chinese-as:
J Edkins wrote A Grammar of Colloquial Chinese, as Exhibited in the Shanghai Dialect, in a second edition corrected, issued at Shanghai by the Presbyterian Mission Press in eighteen sixty eight. A preface to the first edition of eighteen fifty three opens the book. Among works on Chinese grammar, that of Prémare still stands preeminent, he says. Prémare wrote a century and a half before.

Prémare had a better appreciation of the beauties of Chinese style than any other writer, Edkins holds. But his work abounds in good examples while deficient in order and principles, he notes. Remusat used Prémare well but slighted groups of words, he adds. Bazin essay on colloquial Mandarin points the way, he says. His own book takes a limited field, the dialect of a single district. Language students get a pioneer Shanghai dialect grammar.
63330-the-members-of-the-established-chu:
William Geary published The Members of the Established Church Vindicated at Norwich in 1836, a threepence pamphlet. Geary answers a letter on infant education addressed to church members by the Reverend John Alexander, which charged them directly or by hint. In ordinary times he would have let the letter alone; these times were not ordinary.

He lists three charges. The first says the members acted unkindly over arrangements for an exhibition in St Andrew's Hall. The others claim their proposed society would shut out all children but church families, and that a mixed society of all sects would do more public good. The exhibition was Mr Wilderspin's own venture, a show of his infant-school system, and Geary recounts the meetings, the money promised against loss, and the 300 free tickets sent to dissenting congregations. Readers get a parish quarrel of 1836 in full, a window on early schooling politics.
67357-the-missionary-sheriff-being-incid:
The Missionary Sheriff, by Octave Thanet, illustrated by Frost and Carleton, was published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1897. Its subtitle calls the tales incidents in the life of a plain man who tried to do his duty. Six stories fill the contents, closing with The Defeat of Amos Wickliff.

The title story opens with Sheriff Wickliff at his office window, watching the boy soldiers of the Orphans' Home Company march past. He had given most of the money for their uniforms, and their drums and fifes outright. The county court house stands ornate beside the plain yellow stone jail. Under Joe Raker as jailer, window gardens brighten the grim walls all summer. Wickliff is six feet two, with a stiff black mustache and a scar from a Chicago stock yards fight, where he held a mob at bay alone to save a wounded policeman.
68762-chinese-pottery-and-porcelain-vol-:
R L Hobson of the British Museum wrote an account of the potter's art in China from early times to the present day. Volume two, published in 1915, treats Ming and Ch'ing porcelain. The edition was limited to fifteen hundred copies. Forty plates in color and ninety six in black and white illustrate the work.

A front plate shows a covered jar painted with colored enamels, from the early K'ang Hsi period of 1662 to 1722. Chapters follow the Ming dynasty from 1368 to 1644 by reign periods. Hsüan Tê, Ch'êng Hua, and Chia Ching each get close treatment. Hobson marks pieces held by the British Museum with an asterisk.
70766-a-daughter-of-the-samurai:
Etsu Inagaki Sugimoto wrote A Daughter of the Samurai, copyrighted in 1925. Sugimoto taught Japanese language and history at Columbia University. Her subtitle tells the arc: how a daughter of feudal Japan became a modern American.

She opens on winters in Echigo, her home province, where snow lies from December to April. Coolies cut tunnels through the drifts with broad wooden shovels. Chapters follow her schooling, a wedding that never was, her first journey, and how she became a Christian. Later chapters give first impressions of America, a Tokyo home, and a lady of old Japan.
74339-the-sons-of-kai:
Henry Beston retold a Navaho tale, issued in New York in 1926 by Macmillan. The book is given to Mary Cabot Wheelwright, praised for her love of the Southwest and its peoples. Beston sets the tale on the high tableland south and west of the Rocky Mountains.

When a Navaho is ill or well again, friends meet by night for the sacred fire dance. Old men sing the Song of Healing while drums beat and fires sink at dawn. Beston then tells the old tale behind the song. A cliff town in the Canyon de Chelly, twin sons of Kai, and gifts to aid them fill its pages, and a trip home closes it.
76192-land-and-peoples-of-the-kasai:
Land and Peoples of the Kasai is Hilton-Simpson's narrative of a two years' journey in the south-western Congo. Constable published it in London in 1911, with numerous illustrations, eight colour plates, and a map. The frontispiece shows an old Bilumbu relating the legends of his tribe. Chapters run from the coast to the Sankuru river.

The journey passes through the Batetela country and a Bushongo village. The author lives with the Bankutu, whom his title page calls cannibals, and studies the peoples of the great forest. He visits the court of an African king and ascends the Kwilu river. The book records the customs and arts of the Kasai peoples at the height of colonial rule.
7777-narrative-of-the-voyages-round-the-:
Andrew Kippis tells the life of Captain James Cook in this narrative of his voyages round the world, with an account of his years between voyages. Dedicated to the king, it credits royal patronage with making Cook's vast undertakings possible, and with throwing new light on geography, navigation, and science.

The book follows Cook from early service to Pacific discovery, praising a reign that backed learning as well as empire. Through journals, letters, and plain narration, it presents a navigator whose charts and findings reshaped how Britain saw the globe, and whose name became tied to exploration itself.
78968-letters-from-egypt-ethiopia-and-th:
Letters from Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Peninsula of Sinai are travel letters by Richard Lepsius, the Egyptologist. A frontispiece shows Mount Barkal, in the Sudan reach of the Nile, for the book. A transcriber note records that the text was corrected against the German edition from which it was translated. 

Lepsius led the Prussian expedition that surveyed the monuments of Egypt and Nubia in the 1840s. His letters home, written from the field, report temples, inscriptions, and the work of copying them. The Sinai peninsula and the Ethiopian reaches of the Nile extend the route of the volume. Few books did more to found Egyptology as a science of exact record in that century. In letter form the great expedition keeps its human pace: heat, boats, scaffolding, and the slow reading of walls that had waited three thousand years for a reader.
an-englishman-looks-at-the-world-being-a: Herbert George Wells, an Englishman looking at the world, offers unrestrained remarks on contemporary matters, from Blériot's flight to his own first flight. The essays range over politics, science, and daily life with Wells's energy and impatience. They show a prophet of progress taking stock of a changing age.
an-essay-towards-fixing-the-true-standar: Corbyn Morris writes an essay towards fixing the true standards of wit, humour, raillery, satire, and ridicule, dated 1744. The work tries to sort these neighbouring arts, saying what each does well and where each goes wrong. Morris's distinctions give a useful map of eighteenth-century comic theory, sharp and systematic.
britannica-1911-ahai:
Ahai of Sabha, an eighth-century scholar of the Talmud held in high honour, wrote the first Jewish book raised on the Talmud's finished frame. A Talmudist studies the Talmud, the great store of Jewish law and teaching. Ahai's work was the Quaestiones, in Hebrew the Sheiltoth.

The book gathers homilies, lessons in sermon form that treat Jewish law and right conduct. Those lessons pull off a rare trick: they are deep in learning yet plain enough for common hearers, so scholars and folk alike could take them in. That reach helps explain why his name lasts. The landmark claim counts more still. His is set down as the first work by a Jewish scholar penned after the Talmud itself was complete, which lends a short notice a weight well past its size.
britannica-1911-ai:
Ai, a small royal Canaanite city east of Bethel, is examined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name may mean the stone heap, though the word is not necessarily Hebrew. Abraham pitched his tent between Ai and Bethel. The city is chiefly noted, though, for its capture and destruction by Joshua, who made it a heap and a desolation for ever.

Isaiah mentions Ai, and it appears again after the captivity in Ezra and Nehemiah, by then probably no more than a village. Later Hebrew writings give the name feminine forms, Aiath and Aija. Eusebius and Jerome still knew the site, with scanty ruins surviving. The explorer Robinson found no certain traces, but a site south of Deir Diwan, marked by rock-cut reservoirs, tombs, and hewn foundations, is offered as possibly Ai.
britannica-1911-bakalai:
Bakalai are a Bantu tribe of French Congo. Their wide tract lies by the Ogowé river. It stretches south to two degrees latitude. They seem to be immigrants from the south-east. Some link them with the Galoa river people. Neighbouring Fang incursions hurt them badly.

The Bakalai hunt keenly and traded widely. They dealt in rubber and in slaves. French rule has banned the slave traffic. Their women's hairdressing shows great ingenuity. A coiffure can take a whole day. Clay frames and false hair build it up. Red, green, or yellow pigment finishes it. The same colours decorate hut doors. Villages are often dirty, the entry says. Some stand fortified with palisades. Death customs vary by district. Lake Isanga people cremate their dead. Upper Ogowé people use the river instead.
britannica-1911-bakhchi-sarai:
Bakhchi-Sarai is a town in Russia's Taurida government. Its name means garden-palace in Turkish. A narrow Crimean gorge holds it. Simferopol lies 20 miles north-east by rail. From the late 1400s it housed Tatar khans. That residence lasted until 1783.

The town's streets keep an oriental look. Its palace, the Khan-sarai, leads the buildings. Abdul-Sahal-Ghirai erected it in 1519. Fire destroyed it in 1736. Potemkin restored it for Catherine II. A mausoleum holds many khans' tombs. No fewer than thirty-six mosques stand here. Tatars form most of the population. Morocco leather is a local manufacture. Sheepskin cloaks and sabres are made too. The 1897 count gave 12,955 people. Chufut-Kaleh, the old Karaite seat, lies eastward.
britannica-1911-bavai:
Bavai is a town of northern France, in the department of Nord, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies fifteen miles east-south-east of Valenciennes by rail, and held 1622 people in 1906. Its work in the entry's day was the making of iron goods and of fertilizers. Nothing in that modest present hints at its great past, which the short entry is chiefly there to record.

Rome made Bavai's one age of glory. As Bagacum it was the capital of the Nervii, and under Rome a great centre of roads. A milestone marked the meeting place of those roads; it was destroyed in the 1600s and replaced by a column in the 1800s. The barbarian invasions wrecked the town, and it never won back its old weight. It suffered much again in the wars of the 1400s, 1500s, and 1600s, and stayed small.
britannica-1911-caravanserai:
A caravanserai is a public inn for caravans in Asia. It shelters travellers and their animals on the road. Such buildings stand across Asiatic Turkey in particular. This 1911 Britannica article describes the type in detail. A caravanserai usually stands near a town or village. It sits outside the walls, not within them. Its form is a square with a blank outer wall. Small windows sit high in that wall.

Inside, an arcade runs round a central open court. Cell-like store-rooms fill the ground floor level. A lighter arcade above gives access to small lodging rooms. Broad stone stairs join the two storeys. A well with a fountain stands in the court. One great gateway forms the sole entrance to the place. It is wide enough for a loaded camel to pass. Heavy doors and chains guard it at night.
britannica-1911-chand-bardai:
Chand Bardai (flourished about 1200) was a Hindu poet born at Lahore. He lived at the court of Prithwi Raja, the last Hindu king of Delhi. His great work is the Prithiraj Rasau, a poem of some 100,000 stanzas. It tells of his master's deeds and of the events of his time in that part of India. The poem holds worth both as a record of the past and as a work of language.

The Rasau is the first great mark of the Western Hindi tongue. It is also the first of the long line of bardic tales for which Rajputana is famed. The poem is in ballad form. Parts of it are still sung by wandering bards across north-west India and Rajputana. The article points readers to Tod's Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan for good renderings in English.
britannica-1911-chen-hai:
Chên Hai, or Chinhai, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a district town of China, in the province of Cheh Kiang. It stands at the mouth of the Yung kiang, 12 miles north east of Ningpo. The town lies at the foot of a hill on a tongue of land. A dike about three miles long guards it from the sea. The dike is built entirely of large blocks of hewn granite.

The town walls are 20 feet high and three miles in circumference. Its defences were once of considerable strength. They included a well built citadel on a steep cliff 250 feet high, at the tip of the tongue of land. The citadel is now dismantled. In the neighbourhood an engagement took place between the English and Chinese in 1841. The short entry gives a fortified river mouth town, its sea dike, its walls, and the battle that touched it.
britannica-1911-chieng-mai:
Chieng Mai is the capital of the Lao state of the same name and of the Siamese division of Bayap, set on the right bank of the river Me Ping. Massive but decaying walls enclose the town, which stands 800 feet above sea level in a plain ringed by high wooded mountains. Streets cross at right angles, and the palace of the hereditary chief stands inside an inner wall. A fine teak bridge joins the two banks.

Trade has long drawn Chinese, Burmese, Shan and Siamese merchants here, and the town centres the teak trade of Siam. Trade for the division is put at about £2,500,000 a year, and a forest department founded in 1896 has its head office here. Real rule rests with a Siamese high commissioner, though the chief remains nominal ruler. About 20,000 people, mainly Laos, live in the town.
britannica-1911-crowther-samuel-adjai:
Crowther, Samuel Adjai, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an African bishop. Born at Ochugu in the Yoruba country about 1809, he was sold as a slave in 1821. A British warship freed him and many more the next year. He was landed at Sierra Leone and schooled there.

He was baptized in 1825 and became a teacher at Furah Bay. In 1843 he was ordained in England after study at Islington. Back in Africa he worked among his own Yoruba people with success. He made school books and turned the Bible into Yoruba. In 1864 he was made first bishop of the Niger lands. New churches then rose in the Niger delta towns.
britannica-1911-dargai:
Dargai is the name of a mountain peak and a frontier station in the North-West Frontier Province of India. The peak stands on the Samana Range on the Kohat border. It is famous for the stand made there by the Afridis and Orakzais in the Tirah Campaign, and the entry points readers to that campaign's own article for the fighting.

Dargai station itself lies on the Peshawar border. It forms the terminus of the frontier railway that runs from Nowshera to the Malakand Pass. The entry is brief, giving the peak its campaign fame and the station its place at the end of the frontier line, and nothing further.
britannica-1911-haggai:
Haggai, the tenth of the minor prophets in the Old Testament, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His name may mean born on the feast day, though one scholar reads it as a short form of a longer name. Of his own life the Bible tells us next to nothing. Later tales about him are set apart from the facts.

His book holds four short speeches, all given in one autumn. They fall between September and December of the second year of King Darius. That king is held to be Darius Hystaspis, who reigned from 521 to 485 BC. The tone of one speech hints that Haggai was an old man who could recall the years of exile. He worked in Jerusalem at the same time as Zechariah, who then took the lead.
britannica-1911-hai:
Hai was a Jewish lore scholar who lived from nine thirty-nine to ten thirty-eight. He was taught by his father, chief of a famed school, and helped him in his work. Both were cast in gaol for a short time by the caliph. Past his fathers death Hai took his post in nine ninety-eight.

He held that post till his death past forty years on. His fame rests on his words on points of rite and civil law sent to those who asked. He stressed use and old ways where no law was broke. He knew the faith lore of his foes as well.
britannica-1911-hokusai:
Hokusai (1760–1849) was the greatest of the Japanese painters of the Popular School, Ukiyo-ye. He was born at Yedo in the autumn of 1760, the son of a mirror-maker, Nakajima Issai. After practice as a wood-engraver he entered, at eighteen, the studio of Katsugawa Shunshō, a painter and print designer. His disregard for his master's principles got him expelled in 1785, and he kept his independence ever after.

For a time Hokusai lived in extreme poverty, and though his work earned sums that could have brought comfort, he stayed poor and proudly called himself a peasant to the end. He illustrated vast numbers of books, above all the Mangwa, a picture encyclopaedia of Japanese life in fifteen volumes (1812–1875). His Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, forty-six prints in all, were made between 1823 and 1829. Europeans place him among the greatest artists of the world.
britannica-1911-johanan-ben-zaccai:
Joḥanan ben Zaccai was a Palestinian rabbi of the time of the Apostles and a pupil of Hillel. His segment of the hosted file, which also holds the entries for Isaac Jogues and for Johannesburg, names him the chief agent in saving the Jewish faith after Titus destroyed the Temple.

In the Temple's last years he sat in the Sanhedrin. He argued with skill against the Sadducees and belonged to the party of peace in the war with Rome. Seeing the Zealots set on revolt, he had himself carried out of Jerusalem in a coffin. In the Roman camp he won from Vespasian leave to found a college at Jamnia. That college became the centre of Jewish culture and did much of the work of the Sanhedrin. The Mishnah grew from the work begun there.
britannica-1911-kutenai: The Kutenai, or Kutonaga, are a group of North American Indian tribes forming the distinct stock of Kitunahan. Their old range was in British Columbia, along the Kootenay lake and river. They were always friendly to the whites and noted for their honesty. In 1904 there were some 550 of them in British Columbia. In 1908 there were 606 on the Flathead Agency in Montana.
britannica-1911-madvig-johan-nicolai:
Johan Nicolai Madvig, who lived from 1804 to 1886, was a Danish scholar of Latin. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth on the isle of Bornholm. He studied at Frederiksborg school and at Copenhagen. In 1829 he took the chair of Latin language and letters there. He also ran the library of the university. Politics later pulled him into public life.

His party, the Eider Danes, wanted the Eider river as the state border. When it won power he served as head of schooling. He led the Danish parliament from 1856 to 1863. Still, most of his life went to Latin study and school reform. His edition of Cicero's De Finibus, from 1839, changed that field. His Latin grammar for schools spread widely in English dress. Failing sight from 1874 cut his work down. He still lectured, and finished a book on the Roman state before his death.
britannica-1911-mawkmai:
Mawkmai is the subject of a state article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mawkmai is one of the largest states in the southern Shan States of Burma. Its area is given at near twenty eight hundred square miles. The centre of the state is a wide plain, well watered and under rice. The rest is chiefly hills in ranges running north and south. Teak grows in the state but has been badly overworked.

The article says the ruler now works as a contractor for the government. The government takes one third of the net gains from the teak. Rice is the chief crop, but much fine leaf is grown in one district. Cattle breeding is also widespread. In 1901 the people numbered near thirty thousand, over two thirds of them Shans. The capital stands in a fine rice plain. It was burnt by raiders in 1888 but has since recovered.
britannica-1911-shammai:
Shammai is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Jewish scribe of the time of King Herod. Tradition almost always pairs him with Hillel, and the two men stood in striking contrast, in their legal and religious rulings and in character and temper alike. The article notes the irony that the last counsel came from a man known as choleric and brusque.

The piece explains how the rivalry outlived both men. Their opposed views were carried on by their schools, the house of Shammai and the house of Hillel. The article is very short and signed with the initials of its contributor.
britannica-1911-shanghai:
Shanghai, a city in the Chinese province of Kiang su, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The native city stands on the west bank of a river, about twelve miles from where it meets the Yangtsze estuary. Walls ring it, pierced by seven gates.

The entry is harsh on its streets and finds no building of old note in it. A chief suburb stands between the walls and the river, where native shipping lies at anchor. The city forms the main port of central China, with a good anchorage and easy access to the sea. West of it stretches a rich plain cut by waterways and lakes. The goods of that fertile district, plus teas and silks from farther off, find their natural outlet at Shanghai.
britannica-1911-simon-ben-yohai:
Simon ben Yohai is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Galilean Rabbi. He lived in the second century after Christ. He was one of the most eminent pupils of Aqiba. His master was put to death by Hadrian. Simon's own anti-Roman feeling brought him under sentence. That sentence came from Varus about the year 161. He escaped the doom and hid in a cavern for years.

When he came out, he settled in Tiberias. He won fame as a worker of miracles. On that ground he was sent to Rome as an envoy. Legend says he cast a demon out of the emperor's daughter. He bore a large part in the fixing of law. His decisions are often quoted in later works. Great legal homilies were laid to his name. The Zohar was also laid to him, but wrongly. The entry states that claim is altogether unfounded.
britannica-1911-tournai:
Tournai is a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city in the province of Hainaut in Belgium. It stands on the Scheldt river, and its count in 1904 was 36,744. Past sieges and sackings have still left it rich in old works.

The article centres on the cathedral of Notre Dame. Begun in 1030, it joins Romanesque and Gothic work in one grand whole. Five towers with spires crown the pile. A belfry of 1187 stands on the main square near by. In one church lies the tomb of Childeric, found in 1655. Gold bees from that tomb later decked the crown robe of Napoleon. A bridge of 1290, with towers at each end, spans the river. Carpets, caps, and corsets head the trades of the town.
britannica-1911-turgai:
Turgai is a geography article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a vast province of Russian Central Asia in the old Kirghiz steppe. The province covers 176,219 square miles, nearly the size of Caucasia and Transcaucasia together, and belongs to the Aral-Caspian lowland. Two great rivers, the Turgai and the Sary-su, drain toward the Aral basin across it.

The steppe lies only some 300 feet above the sea and is dotted with lakes, the largest of them Chalkar-teniz, which takes in the Turgai river. The climate is harshly dry and continental: January runs as cold as the coast of Novaya Zemlya while July is as hot as July in Morocco. Rain falls under ten inches a year, west winds arrive parched, and summer winds from the north east raise great clouds of sand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abisai:
Abisai, Sarvia's son, Joab's brother, and David's nephew, stands in this entry as one of David's most valiant warriors and most faithful friends. He fought beside David against Saul, then against the Ammonites, Syrians, and Edomites, and later against Absalom, Seba, and the Philistines. The entry follows him through Samuel and Chronicles, marking each campaign with its passage.

His loyalty shows most sharply in the hard moments, when he backs David against rebels and foreign armies alike. The record is short and built almost entirely from scripture citations, with references to Hagen, Palis, and White for readers who want the scholarly background. It presents a soldier defined less by his own story than by steadfast service to his king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adonai:
Adonai, Hebrew for lord or ruler, is a name bestowed on God in the Old Testament, kept in the Vulgate and its dependent versions, at Exodus 6:3 and Judith 16:16. No other name for God is more definite or more easily understood. Etymologically it pluralizes Adon, with the first-person singular possessive suffix.

This plural has drawn various explanations. As a plurale abstractum it would signal the fullness of divine sway, pointing to God as Lord of lords, an explanation Hebrew grammarians endorse, distinguishing a plurale virium or virtutum. Others prefer plurale excellentiae, magnitudinis, or majestatis. It is not a politeness form like German Sie or French vous, and the possessive adds no more meaning than in Rabbi, Monsieur, or Madonna. Adonai also perpetually substitutes for the ineffable name Yahve, lending it vowel signs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aggeus-haggai:
Aggeus, tenth among the Old Testament minor prophets, is called Haggay in Hebrew and Haggaios in the Septuagint, whence Latin Aggeus. His name's meaning is uncertain. Many scholars read it as the festive one, born on a feast day. Others take it as short for Haggiyyah, my feast is Yahweh, a name found in Chronicles.

His personal life is equally uncertain. His book is very short and gives no detail about its author. Its few passages speak only of his divine message delivered in Jerusalem in the second year of Darius I, 520 BC. Jewish tradition, judged to have little historical basis, says he was born in Chaldea during the Captivity, came young to Jerusalem with returning exiles, and was buried among the priests. He has also been wrongly credited with Psalms 111 and 145.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-mai:
Angelo Mai, Roman cardinal and celebrated philologist, was born at Schilpario in Bergamo in 1782 and died at Albano in 1854. Young, he entered the Society of Jesus, was sent to Naples in 1804, and was stationed at Orvieto and Rome. For his skill in palaeography he was appointed in 1811 to the Ambrosian Library at Milan.

This led to his initial discoveries in palimpsests, old manuscripts washed and written over. He found Cicero's orations in 1814 and the correspondence of Fronto, Marcus Aurelius, and Verus in 1815. A speech of Isaeus and a fragment of Plautus's Vidularia followed in 1816, with a Gothic Saint Paul in 1817. He later printed unpublished pages of more than 350 authors, including Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and Origen, and Italian humanists. After long delays he published the Vatican codex, an important Greek Bible manuscript, in 1858. The gall nut he used to revive palimpsest writings half destroyed them, though all reagents injure parchment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-odo-o: Odo of Cambrai, a teacher turned Benedictine abbot and bishop, won fame at Tournai before his stormy tenure at Cambrai. Invited to teach there in 1087, he became a monk in 1095 and abbot of Saint Martin's, then Bishop of Cambrai, consecrated at Reims. Refusing investiture from Emperor Henry IV delayed his possession of the see. Though Henry's son restored it in 1106, Odo was exiled in 1110 and died at Anchin in 1113 without regaining it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cambrai:
Cambrai covers the whole French department of Nord. Before 1559 it was a bishopric of huge reach, taking in even Brussels and Antwerp. The new metropolis of Malines and eleven other dioceses cut it down, and by way of compensation it became an archbishopric with Saint Omer, Tournai, and Namur under it. The Concordat of 1802 reduced it again to a bishopric under Paris.

On Bishop Belmas's death in 1841 it rose once more to an archbishopric, with Arras as suffragan. Its bishops run from Saint Vedulphus, on whose death in 580 the residence moved from Arras to Cambrai. Later names include Saint Gaugericus, Halitgarius, apostle of the Danes, Gerard the Great, who converted the Gondulphian heretics, and Robert of Geneva, antipope in 1378 as Clement VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chusai:
An entry on Chusai the Archite, native of Archi south of Ephraim near Bethel, called in Chronicles the king's friend. That title, like counsellor for Ahitophel or army leader for Joab, was an official rank among the Seleucids for trusted men with military or civil duties, not mere intimacy. In Chusai's case, however, the story of Absalom's rebellion shows the title was more than official.

Just after David learned of Ahitophel's treason, Chusai met him on the Mount of Olives, garments torn and head dusted. David, judging the old man a burden in flight, sent him to Jerusalem to defeat Ahitophel's counsel. Chusai won Absalom's trust, and in council he secured a delay that saved the king, then sent word to David through Zadok, Abiathar, and their sons. Scripture reports his deception without approving it, and the entry asks how far war's ethics can justify it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doctrine-of-a:
The Doctrine of Addai is a Syriac document telling the legend of the conversion of Edessa. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with King Abgar's letter to Christ and the reply, which here is a spoken message with a portrait of Christ, not a letter as Eusebius has it. After the Ascension, Thomas dispatched Addai, counted among the seventy-two disciples, to heal the king and preach at his court.

Addai told of the True Cross found by Protonice, wife of the emperor Claudius, a tale later than Eusebius and built on the story of Saint Helena. The people were converted, and the heathen altars fell. The entry weighs the document's sources and dates, giving readers a window onto the legends of the earliest Syrian church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-douai:
Douai, a town and former university seat in France's Nord department, stands on the River Scarpe, about twenty miles south of Lille. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts about thirty thousand people and notes its strong old ramparts, removed only in recent years. Medieval Douai thrived, and its church of Notre-Dame goes back to the twelfth century.

To English Catholics the name is bound to the college founded by Cardinal Allen under Elizabeth, where most of the clergy were trained in penal times. To that college England owed much of the survival of its Catholic faith. Scots and Irish colleges, with Benedictine and Franciscan houses, joined it, and the entry lists their histories for the reader.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesychius-of-:
Hesychius of Sinai was a Byzantine priest and monk of the Thorn-bush monastery on Mount Sinai and an ascetic author now almost forgotten. Nothing definite is known of his career or the exact time he lived, and only a few fragments of his writings survive, still awaiting collection and separate criticism. In manuscripts he usually bears the honorary title Our Holy Father, which helps tell him apart from other men of the same name.

The key test for his work lies in his Bible quotations, which regularly follow the Codex Sinaiticus, unlike the version used by his namesake of Jerusalem. The pivotal piece is a collection of two hundred ascetic maxims on watchfulness and virtue, printed under the Jerusalem Hesychius in Migne's edition. The entry shows how much of that edition can only be assigned by close monographic study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-de-mo:
Jacques de Molai, also spelled Molay, was born at Rahon, Jura, about 1244. He died at Paris on 18 March 1314. A Templar at Beaune since 1265, he appears as grand master as early as 1298. At trial he called himself an unlettered soldier. Yet he drew on his order's collective experience to preside in 1306 or 1307 over a major crusade plan. He carried it to Poitiers for Clement V, who had summoned him from the East.

Renan judged that plan, built on firsthand knowledge of the Orient and Italian cities, superior to any rival scheme of its age. In it Molai showed full trust in France's king, who soon became his destroyer. At the same time he gave the pope a memorial against merging Hospitallers and Templars, a union debated since Lyons council. The entry presents a soldier-statesman on the eve of his order's fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-nicolai:
Jean Nicolai, a celebrated French Dominican theologian born at Mouzay in 1594 and dead in Paris in 1673. He entered his order at twelve, professed in 1612, and took a Sorbonne doctorate in 1632. He taught philosophy and theology with distinction in many houses, prized for strict observance, prudence, erudition, and penetration.

Nicolai knew Latin, Greek, Italian, Spanish, and Hebrew, sat on the commission examining Jansenist works, and held strictly to Thomist teaching on grace against the Molinists. His books fall in three groups: annotated editions of older theologians, his own theology, and verse and political pieces. Against Jansenists he added a dissertation to each volume of his Pantheologia edition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-molokai:
Molokai, fifth in size among Hawaii's main islands, lies between Oahu and Maui. It is a rugged volcanic island about thirty-eight miles long and seven wide. Cliffs up to 3,500 feet fringe its northern shore. Annexed by the United States in 1898, it counted 2,504 people in the 1900 census. Grazing filled its southern slopes, and a coral reef lined the south coast.

Worldwide fame came through its leper settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula. Father Damien arrived to stay in 1873 and brought order and energy to a struggling community. Franciscan sisters from Syracuse followed in the 1880s. The entry also covers water supply works and the settlement's shift from Kalawao to Kalaupapa. It notes the island's honey, deer and torrent streams.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shammai:
Shammai, called the Elder, was a famous Jewish scribe who, with Hillel, formed the last of the pairs who led the Sanhedrin. Their schools held rival sway, by Talmudic tradition, from about a century before Jerusalem's destruction in 70 AD. The Mishna, the only trustworthy authority here, mentions Shammai in just eight passages. Little else is known with certainty about either great scribe. In character and teaching, Shammai was Hillel's opposite in every way.

He lived the law to the letter with stern severity, pressing legal interpretation to an extreme. The tale is told that when his daughter-in-law bore a child on the feast of Tabernacles, he had the roof broken through. The bed was roofed with boughs, so the infant might keep the feast in a makeshift booth. The strictness of the master marked his school against Hillel's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-of-tour:
Simon of Tournai taught at the University of Paris at the start of the 1200s, with birth and death dates unknown. He was teaching before 1184, since he signed a document alongside Gerard de Pucelle, who died Bishop of Coventry that year. Chroniclers agree on his brilliance in philosophy, which he taught for ten years. Later he lectured on theology with equal success, drawing on Aristotle and other works newly known through Arab translators.

His teachings drew suspicion by the end of the 1100s. Enemies, likely foes of the new philosophy, spread accounts by Thomas de Cantimpré, Matthew Paris, and Giraldus Cambrensis. They differ in detail but agree that Simon was struck dumb for blasphemy or heretical claims. Whether he said in private more than his works contain is now hard to judge. His surviving works, few printed, are orthodox, including a Summa and Sermons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sinai:
Sinai is the mountain where the Mosaic Law was given. Jerome and Gesenius treated Horeb and Sinai as one name, while Ewald, Robinson, and Palmer held Horeb for the whole region around Sinai. The name's origin is disputed, whether from a Hebrew word for desert or for the moon god. The mount was called Sinai, or the mount of God, probably before Moses's day.

The name now covers the triangular peninsula between southern Palestine's desert, the Red Sea, and the gulfs of Aqaba and Suez. It spans about 10,000 square miles, scene of Israel's forty years of wandering after the Exodus. North of Jabal et-Tih stretches an arid plateau cut by wadis, including El-Arish, the River of Egypt. South rises a granite mass split into three groups, western Serbal, central Musa, Catherine, and Um Schomer, and eastern Thebt, peopled by semi-nomadic Arab Muslims under tribal sheikhs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-of-to:
Stephen of Tournai, a canonist, wrote a Summa on Gratian's Decretum that shaped medieval church law. An Orléans man born in 1128, he joined the regular canons of Saint-Euverte there about 1150. He learned canon and Roman law at Bologna and came home to his house in 1160. The canons chose him abbot of Saint-Euverte in 1167, and Paris's Sainte-Geneviève chose him in 1177.

The Paris monastery he almost entirely rebuilt, founding a monastic school beside it. In 1192 he became bishop of Tournai, but popular opposition and the interdict on France over Philip II's divorce proceedings hampered him greatly. His Summa in decretum Gratiani of 1159 draws heavily on Paucapalea, Rufinus, and Rolandus, the future Alexander III, and was first edited by Schulte at Giessen in 1891. His letters fill pages 309 to 625 of volume 111 of the Patrology. He died at Tournai in September 1203.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tournai:
Tournai is a diocese in Belgium, evangelized by St. Piat in the later third century, though he cannot be proved its first bishop. Piat suffered martyrdom under Maximian, and barbarian invasions then wiped out Christian life in the region until the Franks came. Clodion settled at Tournai, Childeric died there in 481, and St. Remigius used Frankish goodwill to organize the northern hierarchy.

Remigius erected the see of Tournai about 500, naming Eleutherius as its bishop. It kept its own bishops for nearly a century, then about 626 its see joined Noyon under one bishop, a union lasting five hundred years. In 1559 Philip II split the vast diocese, taking nearly two-thirds of its land for the new sees of Bruges and Ghent, with six parishes to Ypres. After the Revolution its bounds matched the province of Hainault.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-upper-kassai:
Upper Kassai began as a simple mission in 1901 and was detached as a prefecture apostolic from the Vicariate of Belgian Congo on 20 August 1901. The prefect apostolic lived at the mission of St Joseph de Luluabourg, a few miles south of the Belgian station of Luluabourg. That mission lay in the Lualaba-Kassai district, whose chief town Lusambo housed the district commissioner. At its creation the prefecture covered almost the whole district.

Its bounds ran from the Vicariate of Belgian Congo in the north and east to Portuguese Congo in the south and the Lubue river in the west. In 1908 it grew eastward to the left bank of the Lualaba and westward to a new line. The entry lists its stations, priests, and schools, a brief administrative record of a mission district taking shape in the Belgian Congo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zarai:
Zarai is the Numidian titular see named in the Antonine Itinerary and the Peutinger Table. Ptolemy calls it Zaratha and wrongly places it in Mauretania Caesariensis; it is probably Apuleius's Zaratha too. The forms Zaratha and Zaraitani, found in inscriptions, suggest the name Zarai on another inscription lost a final dental letter. Its ruins, Henshir Zaria, southeast of Setif in Algeria, crown a height commanding the left bank of the Oued Taourlatent, which medieval Arabs called Oued Zaraoua.

Remains of a Byzantine citadel and two Christian basilicas are still visible there. Only two bishops of Zarai are known: Cresconius, present at Carthage's conference in 411 against the Donatist rival Rogatus. Adeodatus, exiled by Huneric after Carthage's conference in 484, died in exile for the faith. The entry draws on Smith's Greek and Roman geography, Müller's notes on Ptolemy, Toulotte's Christian Africa, and Diehl's Byzantine Africa.
comrades-of-the-saddle-or-the-young-roug:
Comrades of the Saddle; Or, The Young Rough Riders of the Plains, by Frank V. Webster, was copyrighted in 1910 by Cupples & Leon. Two boys hurry home through twilight outside the town of Bramley as the tale opens. Twenty-five chapters of ranch adventure follow: the Half-Moon Ranch, a race in the moonlight, a message from Cross-Eyed Pete.

Mr. Wilder's ranch is the base, and Gus Megget, Nails, and Jeffreys ride its business. The chapter titles promise the plot's turns: preparations for pursuit, out on the plains, a terrible plot, the prairie fire, a ride for life, and capturing the cattle thieves. Word comes from the West that leasing the bottom lands has spoiled a criminal trade. Homeward ends the campaign.
doe-osti-2589582-machine-learning-models:
Brian Chen, in Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11868R, studies how to speed up a common hard problem in engineering design. Many designs must be optimized while obeying partial differential equations, the math that governs flow, heat, and stress. Solving those equations inside every design trial is slow, so the report tests machine learning stand-ins that answer much faster.

One route places Gaussian process models, which also estimate their own uncertainty, inside trust region methods that accept steps cautiously. Another builds neural network solvers that learn to satisfy the governing equations directly, including randomized Fourier networks with a correction term. Tests include tracking a moving density that starts as a standard bell curve, using flow-based networks with eight coupling layers. The methods aim at design loops that stay accurate without full physics runs at every step.
doe-osti-3006734-fair-surrogate-benchmar:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0021419 covers the FAIR Surrogate Benchmarks project, which built a community repository for benchmarks of AI surrogate models in high-performance computing. Geoffrey Fox of the University of Virginia was lead principal investigator; Piotr Luszczek led at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville for 2020 to 2023, then Mark Gates for 2024. Deep learning surrogates can replace part or all of a large simulation and run orders of magnitude faster, saving compute time and energy.

The Surrogate Benchmark Initiative team spanned Argonne, Indiana University, Rutgers, UTK, and UVA. Its repositories hold data, code, and all files needed to reuse each benchmark, organized on FAIR principles: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. One highlighted result, the SpikeRL framework for spiking neural network reinforcement learning, ran 4.26 times faster and 2.25 times more energy efficiently than prior state-of-the-art methods, with open-source code released.
doe-osti-3012635-carbon-capture-pilot-at:
RTI International's final technical report, dated January 12, 2026, is the Phase 1 performance report for a carbon capture pilot at the Vicksburg Containerboard Mill. The work ran under award DE-CD0000051 from the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations. Vijay Gupta served as principal investigator. The report follows the standard progress format: schedule, budget, procurement, design, and community benefits.

Much of the period's work went into project frameworks rather than construction. A safety and security framework was written and accepted by DOE. Its terms, cyber provisions included, were passed down to subcontractors. Several tasks show no further progress. Permitting and community characterization are among them. The team had turned to securing an alternate host site for the pilot.
doe-osti-3021453-scalable-ai-optimizatio:
X-ScaleSolutions research progress report for DOE SBIR Phase I grant DE-SC0025980, by project lead Soham Ghosh, dated March 3, 2026, covers the project's first year, February 2025 to February 2026. Training and running large language models and computer vision models is costly, and finding their best settings, the hyperparameters, multiplies the cost. DeepHyper automates that search, while the firm's X-ScaleAI framework runs spread-out training, but the two were not yet linked.

The interim report tells of the joining work: linking DeepHyper's automated tuning to X-ScaleAI's training and deployment pipelines across unlike computing setups. A technology assistance report surveys the path to market, citing market analyses for sectors from healthcare analytics to e-commerce logistics. The goal is a single workflow where tuning a model is as routine as training it, cutting wasted compute for model builders.
doe-osti-3376725-criteria-for-retention-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-25423, issued July 1, 2026, sets rules for which plutonium storage cans may stay at the Savannah River Site. Elizabeth J. Kelly, Stephen Hensel, Josh Narlesky, and Theodore Venetz wrote it. The cans are model 3013, the standard steel vessel for storage of plutonium-bearing stock. One group, coded S1, holds more water than the norm: over 0.08 percent by weight. Thirty-three cans were put up for a longer stay.

The rest of the S1 stock will be blended down and thrown out by the end of 2028. Field checks and shelf-life data say no can in the group should fail inside its fifty-year term. Rust risk varies can to can. Experts scored each can, and a model ties that score to damp, salt traces, and scrap type. The model catches about half the spread in scores, a gap the authors flag plainly.
doe-osti-3384923-crada-number-nfe-22-093:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2026/4628, by Kim Tutin of the Manufacturing Science Division and dated December 2025, closes agreement NFE-22-09315 with Captis Aire LLC. The volume follows the standard closeout shape. It has an abstract, a statement of objectives, and the benefits to the funding office's mission. A technical discussion of work performed by all parties follows. Subject inventions, commercialization possibilities, and plans for future collaboration close it.

One figure is personal. It shows Tutin accepting the United States Environmental Protection Agency's Green Chemistry Challenge Award, a marker of what the collaboration produced. CRADA finals are deliberately plain documents. Their job is to put the partnership, the work, and any inventions on the public record in five pages. This one does that for the Captis Aire project.
doe-osti-3995273-evaluation-of-artificia:
Corinne G. Roth, William J. Hutton, Fleurdeliza A. de Peralta, and Adam Baji of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory weigh how well smart software can read bills of materials. Their report, PNNL-39767, is dated September 2026. A bill of materials lists every part in a product, and such lists drive buying, repair, and supply checks.

Parts in a list lean on each other, so a good method must weigh both the whole list's likeness to others and the web of links inside it. Graph methods, clustering, and language models are among the routes weighed. A method that works in one field, such as network switches, should carry to others if it reads the list itself with care. Supply teams get a sober guide to which tools fit this data, and what proof to ask for before trusting them.
froudacity-west-indian-fables-by-james-a:
J. J. Thomas's Froudacity, printed in 1889, answers James Anthony Froude's travel book on the British West Indies point by point. Thomas, a Trinidad schoolmaster and scholar, read Froude in Grenada and saw, under the rhetorical flowers, a scheme to deny the colonies elected legislatures. Froude argued that the islands' African majority made self-government a menace to civilization. Thomas's preface names that argument plainly and promises to dismantle it with Froude's own pages.

Inside, the four books follow Froude island by island: Barbados, St. Vincent, Grenada, then Trinidad at length. Thomas corrects scenes, statistics, and portraits of Black workers, clergy, and voters as he goes. A historical summary closes the case for West Indian capacity and confederation. Readers get a landmark of Caribbean letters, a colonial subject writing back to a famous historian in his own language, and winning the argument on evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrazierWBCaptai:
Dallas Police Captain W. B. Frazier gave the FBI a set of statements about a dangerous duty. His subject was the threats made against prisoner Lee Harvey Oswald and the security planned for Oswald's transfer on November 24, 1963. That transfer is the one Jack Ruby broke through to shoot Oswald on live television.

After Ruby's shot, every security decision was re-examined. The captain who helped arrange the move had to explain the threats he knew of and the precautions taken. His statements preserve the police account of a failure that happened in front of the whole country.
narrative-of-the-voyages-round-the-world:
Andrew Kippis tells the life and voyages of Captain James Cook here. Kippis dedicates the book to the King with high praise. Royal bounty, he says, made Cook's vast undertakings possible. Without it, the world would lack vast new light on geography.

Cook's three voyages round the world form the book's core. Kippis also covers Cook's life between and before the voyages. He credits the King's support of science for an age of knowledge. The narrative made Cook's fame plain to common readers. It stands as an early, full life of the navigator who redrew the Pacific map.
nasa-tm-19660017562-some-results-concern:
Edith I Reed at Goddard and Jacques E Blamont of the national research center in Paris reported results on the airglow as seen from the OGO-II satellite. Airglow is a faint light the upper air gives off at all hours. Its main spectral lines carry facts about the gases that emit them. A corrected copy of the paper is dated 1966 in the sample.

Measuring airglow from a satellite avoids the glow's being drowned by ground lights and haze. Each line points to a certain gas at a certain height. Reed and Blamont present some results on those principal lines. International teamwork on a United States satellite was itself a mark of the era's space science.
nasa-tm-19700022586-experimental-evaluat:
Edward R. Furman of the Lewis Research Center led this study, with Robert D. Brooks and R. W. Harrison of the General Electric Company in Cincinnati. Their paper was written for a 1970 energy conversion conference in Las Vegas. It evaluates mercury boilers for the SNAP-8 power system.

The boilers were built from tantalum joined to stainless steel. In the SNAP-8 design, a boiler turns liquid mercury into vapor that drives a turbine. Tests judged how well these boilers worked and held up. SNAP-8 was a nuclear power system meant to supply electricity on long space missions.
nasa-tm-19710017498-a-reference-atmosphe:
E A Carter and S C Brown of the Marshall Space Flight Center issued this reference on May 10, 1971, as NASA TM X-64590. Both worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. The book gives a standard atmosphere for Vandenberg Air Force Base in California. This is the annual version for 1971. Launch teams on the West Coast used Vandenberg for polar orbit missions.

A reference atmosphere lists expected air values by height. The tables cover heat, pressure, and density through the air column. Engineers feed those values into flight and reentry calculations. A shared standard keeps every team's math on the same footing. The catalog record notes the tables rest on a current annual tabulation.
nasa-tm-19710079289-an-investigation-of-:
Raymond M. Hicks, Joel P. Mendoza, and Lionel L. Levy Jr. of the Ames Research Center wrote this investigation, NASA TM X-62,030, on sonic booms from returning space shuttle orbiters. A reentering orbiter drags a boom carpet across the ground below its flight path. Planners needed to know how strong that boom would be before choosing an orbiter shape.

Wind tunnel tests measured boom overpressure for two shapes: a straight-wing orbiter and a delta-wing orbiter. Two reentry trajectories were analyzed for the delta design and one for the straight wing. The authors found that trajectory and angle of attack both strongly affect the boom level under the flight path. A gentler, constant angle of attack for the delta orbiter kept the overpressure low. It stayed under about one pound per square foot across the speeds tested.
tanakh-jps-1917-haggai:
Haggai is a brief prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the 1917 English of the Jewish Publication Society. Its words are dated to the second year of Darius the king and sent to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, and Joshua the high priest.

The charge is plain: the people live in fine roofed houses while God's house still lies in ruins. Their fields yield little, their pay leaks away like coins in a holed bag, and rain is held back. Haggai urges them to haul wood from the hills and build. Readers get a short, sharp call to put shared worship first after exile, with drought read as a sign of misplaced care.
the-hawaiian-romance-of-laieikawai: Martha Warren Beckwith supplied the introduction and translation for The Hawaiian Romance of Laieikawai. The contents list study sections on the persons, action, and background of the story, followed by the text and translation in twenty-seven chapters. Chapter titles trace the birth of the Princess, her flight to Paliuli, suitors who seek her, a boxing match with Cold-nose, and a journey to the Heavens. Front matter is all that is present here.
the-scouts-of-stonewall-the-story-of-the:
Joseph A. Altsheler's The Scouts of Stonewall retells the great Valley campaign as a story. His foreword calls it an independent story. In effect, though, it continues a series. That series began with The Guns of Bull Run and went on with The Guns of Shiloh. This romance returns to the Southern side, Altsheler says.

The book follows Harry Kenton and his friends. A character list introduces Harry as a lad fighting for the South. His cousin Dick Mason fights for the North. Colonel George Kenton is Harry's father. Colonel Leonidas Talbot commands the Invincibles, a Southern regiment. Lieutenant Colonel Hector St. Hilaire is his second in command. Other figures include a Northern spy, William J. Shepard. A Vermont youth who loves mathematics, George Warner, also appears.
